Let’s break this down step by step.  

The premise says:  
> Nobody is neither an owner of a The Body Shop soap nor a frequent consumer of Lush soap.  

Let:  
- \( A \) = "owner of a The Body Shop soap"  
- \( B \) = "frequent consumer of Lush soap"  

"Neither A nor B" means: \(\neg A \land \neg B\)  
"Nobody is neither A nor B" means: \(\neg \exists x (\neg A(x) \land \neg B(x))\)  
This is equivalent to: \(\forall x (A(x) \lor B(x))\) — everyone is either an owner of The Body Shop soap or a frequent consumer of Lush soap (or both).  

The conclusion says:  
> Nobody is neither a frequent consumer of Lush soap nor an owner of a The Body Shop soap.  

"Neither B nor A" means: \(\neg B \land \neg A\)  
"Nobody is neither B nor A" means: \(\neg \exists x (\neg B(x) \land \neg A(x))\)  
This is equivalent to: \(\forall x (B(x) \lor A(x))\) — everyone is either a frequent consumer of Lush soap or an owner of The Body Shop soap (or both).  

But \(A(x) \lor B(x)\) is logically equivalent to \(B(x) \lor A(x)\) (commutativity of disjunction).  

So the premise and conclusion are exactly the same statement in different word order.  

If the premise is true, the conclusion must be true — it’s the same proposition.  

Therefore, the argument is **deductively valid**.  

Final answer: valid
